docs.intro: What each part of the product does, and where its full contract lives in the repository.
docs.theme.projects.title: Projects
docs.theme.projects.body: An organisation-scoped workspace tied to a GitHub repository. Runs started against a project are kept together, and finished artifacts can be published back to that repository.
docs.theme.runs.title: Runs
docs.theme.runs.body: One goal driven through the plan → validate → execute → validate supervision loop. The timeline in this visualizer reads newest first, and a cancelled run is not the same thing as a failed one.
docs.theme.registry.title: Registry
docs.theme.registry.body: The one tier-keyed table of agent identity: every Molecule, Cell and Tissue that has run, its name, version history and the trust it has earned. Trust earned here is what lets repeat work skip to a cheaper path next time.
docs.theme.skills.title: Skills
docs.theme.skills.body: A persistent task recipe an agent earns credit for and compiles once trusted, kept under its owning agent's namespace. A skill review shown here is a mechanical pre-screen only — never a sharing approval.
docs.theme.burnin.title: Burn-in
docs.theme.burnin.body: A batch of real tasks run end to end to measure defects, cost and friction before a release. What is shown here is the last recorded batch, not a live guarantee about the next one.
docs.theme.launch.title: Launch
docs.theme.launch.body: How to phrase a goal for a run. In an organisation, connect your agent to Atoma MCP and ask it to draft the goal from your conversation and repository context. A local instance with no organisations has no projects: start a run from a shell with `npm run run:build -- "<goal>"`.
docs.theme.admin.title: Admin
docs.theme.admin.body: Five screens behind the platform-admin flag: organisations with their members and one-use invitations, the platform audit journal (the one source of what happened on this deployment), the catalogue ledger of what the agent catalogue learned, the sentinel — the mechanical live watch over runs in flight — and announcements, the one push a human writes, reviewed in every supported language before it leaves. An invitation never grants operator-level access.
docs.theme.mcp.title: MCP
docs.theme.mcp.body: One Streamable HTTP control plane on /mcp for host applications such as Claude Code or Codex, showing each caller the atoma_* tools its role admits. These are read APIs plus run-starters driven as MCP tasks, not agent elements — global concurrency is configurable (10 by default), with one active run per organisation.
docs.user.intro: Practical guidance for delivery teams, from business brief to reviewable GitHub hand-off.
docs.user.quick.title: From business outcome to reviewable software
docs.user.quick.lede: Atoma turns one scoped request into a runnable, self-contained software artifact. Each run decomposes, executes and verifies the work, records estimated usage and cost, and keeps the GitHub publication receipt separate from the delivery verdict.
docs.user.quick.flow.title: The five-step working loop
docs.user.quick.flow.intro: You own the outcome and the acceptance decision. Atoma owns the supervised execution record in between.
docs.user.quick.flow.scope.title: Choose the project
docs.user.quick.flow.scope.body: Ask your connected agent to use the project that owns this workstream, its repository and its delivery history.
docs.user.quick.flow.brief.title: Brief one outcome
docs.user.quick.flow.brief.body: Have your agent draft one artifact or bounded change with observable acceptance criteria, then review the goal.
docs.user.quick.flow.run.title: Run the work
docs.user.quick.flow.run.body: Approve the goal, then let your agent start the run through Atoma MCP. Atoma plans, builds and verifies in an isolated project container.
docs.user.quick.flow.evidence.title: Inspect evidence
docs.user.quick.flow.evidence.body: Verification, model and tool activity, duration, tokens and estimated cost remain traceable.
docs.user.quick.flow.handoff.title: Confirm the hand-off
docs.user.quick.flow.handoff.body: Review the result and the separate GitHub commit receipt before your team adopts the output.
docs.user.quick.fit.title: Choose work Atoma can finish well
docs.user.quick.fit.good.title: Small, self-contained software
docs.user.quick.fit.good.body: Single-page web tools, Node HTTP JSON APIs, CLI utilities, configuration and technical documentation. Every required input must be available to the run.
docs.user.quick.fit.split.title: Work with external dependencies
docs.user.quick.fit.split.body: Break down multi-system rollouts, production migrations and policy decisions. A first run cannot import an existing repository or reach services, credentials or data outside its workspace.
docs.user.quick.rule.title: Keep each decision reviewable
docs.user.quick.rule.body: Use one run for one outcome that a reviewer can accept or reject. Ask for the next change in a follow-up run; the project keeps both the working state and the evidence history together.
docs.user.projects.title: Give every stream of work a durable home
docs.user.projects.lede: A project belongs to the active organisation, targets one GitHub repository and groups every run made against that workstream. Later runs resume the latest delivered or partial workspace. Projects imported from GitHub start from the current default branch instead; unpublished partial changes are not reused.
docs.user.projects.anatomy.title: What a project keeps together
docs.user.projects.anatomy.stream.title: One shared delivery context
docs.user.projects.anatomy.stream.body: Use a clear name for the client engagement, internal product or operational utility the team will recognise later.
docs.user.projects.anatomy.repo.title: One GitHub destination
docs.user.projects.anatomy.repo.body: Each project owns one repository target. A delivered run is published automatically, and the project shows whether that publication reached GitHub.
docs.user.projects.anatomy.history.title: Incremental runs, one history
docs.user.projects.anatomy.history.body: The first run starts from an empty workspace. Each later run starts from the previous delivered workspace, so changes build on earlier work.
docs.user.projects.patterns.title: Project patterns for B2B teams
docs.user.projects.patterns.intro: Choose a boundary that makes repository ownership and review responsibility obvious.
docs.user.projects.patterns.consulting.b: Use a dedicated private project for one client deliverable or accelerator, then make each milestone a separate run.
docs.user.projects.patterns.product.body: Keep a small tool, interface or API in one project and request reviewable changes run by run.
docs.user.projects.patterns.operations.b: Keep a calculator, converter, reporting CLI or technical document with the team that owns its rules and review.
docs.user.projects.visibility.title: Prefer private for client and internal work
docs.user.projects.visibility.body: Public repositories are readable by anyone and the choice cannot be changed later in Atoma. Private is the default and the safer starting point for non-public work.
docs.user.projects.access.title: Read-only roles can still review
docs.user.projects.access.body: Project creation and run starts happen through your connected agent. A viewer role can inspect projects, runs, costs, evidence and publication receipts, but needs member access to start work.
docs.user.goals.title: Write goals teams can test and review
docs.user.goals.lede: A strong goal describes one observable outcome, not the agent workflow. Give Atoma the artifact shape, required behaviour, acceptance criteria and only the constraints that truly matter.
docs.user.goals.formula.title: The four-part goal formula
docs.user.goals.formula.intro: Write these four parts in business language. Atoma chooses the tools, phases and verification method from the artifact's nature.
docs.user.goals.formula.artifact.title: Artifact
docs.user.goals.formula.artifact.body: Name the shape: a single HTML page, Node HTTP JSON API, CLI, configuration or technical document.
docs.user.goals.formula.behaviour.title: Behaviour
docs.user.goals.formula.behaviour.body: Describe inputs, outputs, user actions, routes, status codes or calculations that a reviewer can observe.
docs.user.goals.formula.acceptance.title: Acceptance
docs.user.goals.formula.acceptance.body: State required states and important error cases. Replace vague quality words with concrete outcomes.
docs.user.goals.formula.constraints.body: Name hard limits such as dependency policy, file format, compatibility or scope. Keep every required input self-contained.
docs.user.goals.example.title: Maintenance work-order API
docs.user.goals.example.body: Build a dependency-free Node HTTP JSON API for maintenance work orders. Support GET and POST /work-orders; require assetId and priority; return 400 when either field is missing; keep records in memory and return 404 for an unknown id.
docs.user.goals.quality.title: Make the brief useful to both builder and reviewer
docs.user.goals.quality.do.title: Bound the observable result
docs.user.goals.quality.do.body:
• Ask for one outcome
• Include important edge cases
• Supply every required input
• State what must remain unchanged
• Use domain language your reviewer knows
docs.user.goals.quality.avoid.title: Do not prescribe the workflow
docs.user.goals.quality.avoid.body:
• Several unrelated deliverables
• Vague requests such as make it modern
• Tool names, phases or verification commands
• Missing files, credentials or external data
• Open-ended research programmes
docs.user.runs.title: See how the work is being done
docs.user.runs.lede: Runs shows a causal timeline rather than a delivery banner alone. Follow live progress, then inspect the result, verification evidence, model and tool activity, branches, duration, tokens and estimated cost.
docs.user.runs.status.title: Read the status before the detail
docs.user.runs.status.live.title: Still executing
docs.user.runs.status.live.body: The view refreshes while work continues. Timeline events are shown newest first.
docs.user.runs.status.delivered.title: Supervision accepted the artifact
docs.user.runs.status.delivered.body: Review the evidence and confirm the separate publication receipt before hand-off.
docs.user.runs.status.failed.title: No accepted deliverable
docs.user.runs.status.failed.body: Read the error, result and final timeline events before deciding whether to reframe or retry.
docs.user.runs.status.cancelled.title: Stopped by request
docs.user.runs.status.cancelled.body: Cancellation is recorded separately from failure, so it does not misstate what happened.
docs.user.runs.read.title: Review a run in this order
docs.user.runs.read.intro: Start with the decision-level evidence. Move into the timeline only when you need to understand how the result was produced.
docs.user.runs.read.result.title: Result
docs.user.runs.read.result.body: Open Result to read and copy the final answer or download its JSON. Published files link to that run’s exact GitHub revision. In Projects, open the latest delivered result or choose Result on any historical run. Partial results are labelled separately from completed deliveries.
docs.user.runs.read.proof.title: Ground truth
docs.user.runs.read.proof.body: Check observed files and the browser, API or CLI probes that match the artifact.
docs.user.runs.read.summary.title: Summary
docs.user.runs.read.summary.body: Review duration, calls, tokens, cache use, estimated cost and any fallback or degraded warning.
docs.user.runs.read.timeline.title: Timeline
docs.user.runs.read.timeline.body: Inspect plans, prompts, responses, tool arguments and results, validations, branches, trust and cache events.
docs.user.runs.layers.title: The roles you see in the timeline
docs.user.runs.layers.intro: The names make responsibility attributable. You brief the outcome; Atoma chooses and records the specialised roles.
docs.user.runs.layers.tissue.title: Decomposes the goal
docs.user.runs.layers.tissue.body: Frames the top-level phases and how their outputs belong together.
docs.user.runs.layers.cell.title: Routes and validates
docs.user.runs.layers.cell.body: Chooses a focused worker for each phase and reviews plans and results.
docs.user.runs.layers.molecule.title: Builds with Elements
docs.user.runs.layers.molecule.body: The only rank that invokes tools to write, run and probe the artifact.
docs.user.runs.notifications.section: Stay informed without keeping the tab open
docs.user.runs.notifications.title: Know when your run and publication finish
docs.user.runs.notifications.body: When the browser offers notifications on your first live run, enable them to receive the final run status and the later GitHub publication outcome for work you requested.
docs.user.review.title: Turn a delivered run into an accountable decision
docs.user.review.lede: Atoma can verify an artifact and record how it was produced. Your team still decides whether the result satisfies the business need and is safe for its intended environment.
docs.user.review.gate.title: Three checks before hand-off
docs.user.review.gate.evidence.title: Evidence matches the goal
docs.user.review.gate.evidence.body: Compare the requested behaviour with the result, phase breakdown and ground-truth observations.
docs.user.review.gate.repository.title: GitHub has the expected result
docs.user.review.gate.repository.body: Confirm the publication status and commit SHA, then review the repository diff and declared output set.
docs.user.review.gate.signoff.title: A human owns adoption
docs.user.review.gate.signoff.body: Apply your domain, security, policy and target-environment checks before release or client delivery.
docs.user.review.checklist.title: Make the hand-off explicit
docs.user.review.checklist.body:
• Requested behaviour is present and bounded
• Ground-truth evidence matches the artifact
• Failed, fallback or degraded paths are understood
• Estimated cost is acceptable
• Published commit is the expected hand-off
• Target-environment review is complete
docs.user.review.boundary.section: Three words that must stay distinct
docs.user.review.boundary.title: A verdict is not a production approval
docs.user.review.boundary.body: Delivered means supervision accepted the artifact. Published means GitHub recorded it. Neither means your organisation approved the result for production, regulatory use or an external client.
docs.user.playbooks.title: Repeatable patterns for product, industry and consulting teams
docs.user.playbooks.lede: Use Atoma where a small software artifact can make a bounded business rule executable and reviewable. Keep the project boundary, run cadence and human owner explicit.
docs.user.playbooks.patterns.title: Three practical starting points
docs.user.playbooks.patterns.intro: These are software-scoped patterns, not promises to operate a business process or production system on your behalf.
docs.user.playbooks.consulting.title: Prototype with a client-ready audit trail
docs.user.playbooks.consulting.body:
Pattern: one private project per delivery stream, one run per reviewable milestone.

Example: Build a single-page intake dashboard from embedded sample data, with status filters, totals and a print-ready summary.
docs.user.playbooks.product.title: Iterate on a small internal product
docs.user.playbooks.product.body:
Pattern: establish one artifact, then request one behaviour change per follow-up run.

Example: Build a Node JSON API for feature requests with create, list and status-update routes plus explicit 400 and 404 cases.
docs.user.playbooks.industry.title: Make an operational rule executable
docs.user.playbooks.industry.body:
Pattern: encode a bounded calculation or transformation without connecting to production systems.

Example: Build a CLI that reads a maintenance CSV and prints downtime and intervention count per asset, rejecting invalid rows.
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.title: A reviewable delivery cadence
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.frame.title: Frame
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.frame.body: Choose one owner, artifact and acceptance decision.
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.deliver.body: Run the bounded brief and let artifact-specific probes execute.
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.review.title: Review
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.review.body: Inspect evidence, estimated cost and the GitHub commit.
docs.user.playbooks.cadence.iterate.body: Use the next run for the next bounded change, preserving history.
docs.user.trust.title: Know what Atoma proves and where humans decide
docs.user.trust.lede: Traceability makes review possible; it does not remove judgment. Treat the run record as technical evidence and the published repository as a hand-off, not as a compliance certificate.
docs.user.trust.boundary.title: Shared responsibility
docs.user.trust.boundary.intro: Keep machine-observed facts and human accountability on their proper sides of the boundary.
docs.user.trust.boundary.atoma.title: Execution and technical evidence
docs.user.trust.boundary.atoma.body:
• Goal, plans and routing
• Model and tool events
• Validation and ground truth
• Duration, tokens and estimated cost
• Status and publication receipt
docs.user.trust.boundary.team.title: Business acceptance and release
docs.user.trust.boundary.team.body:
• Approved input data
• Domain correctness
• Security and compliance review
• Repository and client review
• Production deployment and monitoring
docs.user.trust.data.title: Data and execution hygiene
docs.user.trust.data.secrets.title: Keep credentials out of the goal
docs.user.trust.data.secrets.body: Do not place passwords, API keys, private tokens or production credentials in prompts or generated project files.
docs.user.trust.data.trace.title: Treat traces as project records
docs.user.trust.data.trace.body: Goals, prompts, responses and tool output may be stored in the trace and read by authorised organisation users and the platform operator.
docs.user.trust.data.container.title: Bring self-contained inputs
docs.user.trust.data.container.body: Project runs execute in a container with outbound networking disabled. The run cannot fetch a repository, service or dataset from the internet.
docs.user.trust.limits.tag: USE THE EVIDENCE, NOT A MARKETING GUARANTEE
docs.user.trust.limits.title: Small software artifacts, bounded concurrency
docs.user.trust.limits.body: Atoma does not certify regulatory compliance, guarantee correctness or cost savings, enforce a cost ceiling, import an existing codebase or deploy to production. Global concurrency is configurable (10 project runs by default), with one active run per organisation. Requests beyond the global limit wait in a queue and start automatically when a slot becomes available.
admin.empty: No organisation yet. The first login creates one.
admin.invitationCopied: The link was copied to your clipboard. It is a one-use credential shown only here.
admin.ledgerHint: What the agent catalogue learned: every trust and lifecycle change of an agent type or a skill recipe — a separate record from the platform journal.
admin.ledgerEmpty: The catalogue has learned nothing yet.
journal.scrollHint: Scrolling to the bottom loads the next page.
sentinel.title: Sentinel
sentinel.watch.scope: This server hosts the watch, so it reports its own timer — and only its own. A sentinel on another machine, or against another store, is invisible here.
sentinel.watch.armed_one: Watching, one pass every second since {{since}}.
sentinel.watch.disabled: Not watching: ATOMA_VIZ_SENTINEL=0 on this server.
sentinel.watch.leaseHeld: {{source}} pid {{pid}} has held the watch on this store since {{since}} (last beat {{beat}}). One appending watch per store, so this server yielded.
sentinel.watch.leaseLost: This server lost the watch: something took this store over. It will take it back on its own once that watch stops.
sentinel.watch.failing_one: Stopped after one failed pass. Last error: {{error}}
sentinel.watch.failing_other: Stopped after {{count}} failed passes in a row. Last error: {{error}}
sentinel.watch.slow: That pass took {{ms}}ms, and it runs on the HTTP loop. A trace this large is worth looking at.
sentinel.watch.headless: A watch without a browser: npm run sentinel
sentinel.coverageEmpty: No run in flight. Nothing to watch this second.
sentinel.findingsEmpty: No finding recorded. Nothing has been flagged.
sentinel.flagOnly: A finding is a flag, never a judgment: nothing here can cancel a run.
sentinel.rule.cost-alert: Cumulative spend passed the operator threshold. An alert, not a budget — nothing refuses to spend past it.
sentinel.rule.identical-tool-streak: The same element called with byte-identical arguments, over and over: a stall, not a retry.
sentinel.rule.recurring-tool-error: One element failing repeatedly with the same error. Read in two places: the transport exception and the element’s own ok:false.
sentinel.rule.slow-tool-outlier: One call far slower than the median for that same element name, with at least three samples.
sentinel.rule.injection-signature: An injection signature in an element RESULT — where untrusted content enters. A screen that says where to look, never an authorization boundary.
sentinel.rule.trajectory-drift: One closed Molecule execution whose ordered element sequence sits far from every credited execution of the same Molecule and skill in finished runs, once three are known. Uncalibrated: a row to read, never a judgment.
registry.detailInstructionHint: Composed per call from the task, the plan and any injected skills — so it belongs to a run, not to the agent type. Open an LLM event in Runs to read the one that was actually sent.
registry.detailFallbackElementsHint: Used only for last-resort execution when delegation fails. Normal planning and validation have no element access.
registry.runActor.badge: Run actor · not an agent type
registry.runActor.root: The run's final judge. When the work is done it decides whether the delivery meets the request: mechanical gates, ground-truth probes, the proof floor and the acceptance checklist, then a validation call when one of them asks for review. A refusal sends the run back for one repair pass; a second refusal keeps the work as partial.
registry.runActor.criteria: Reviews the acceptance criteria during the final check, a few at a time, against evidence the host collected — never against the run's own report.
registry.runActor.textReference: Writes its own answer to a text request without seeing the delivery, so the final check can compare the two.
registry.runActor.checklist: Drafts the acceptance checklist once, before the first attempt: the outcomes a finished delivery must show.
registry.runActor.router: Picks the top-level tissue the run enters through, or asks for a new one when none fits.
registry.runActor.tissueAuthor: Writes a new reusable tissue for the platform catalogue when the router finds none that fits.
registry.runActor.whyHeading: Why there is no agent sheet
registry.runActor.why: The run makes this call itself. It is not in the registry, so it has no ordinal, version, provenance, stored prompt, elements or trust counters. Its prompt is fixed in code: open one of its LLM events to read the one that was sent.
registry.runActor.tier: Recorded as L{{tier}}: the rank it speaks for in the hierarchy, not the model it runs on.
registry.runActor.noCalls: No LLM call recorded in this trace.
registry.unrecorded.body: This run names the agent type, but its trace holds no registry snapshot of it, so its definition cannot be shown as it was. Open it in Registry to read its current definition.

settings.mcpTransportHint: This address is for an MCP client, not a web page. Opening it in a browser does not test the connection. Keep the /mcp path; do not use /api/tokens as the server address.
settings.mcpCompatibility: Atoma supports browser OAuth sign-in and manual Bearer API tokens. Your agent requests access separately from your website session; approve the connection in the browser.
settings.mcpLocalHint: This is a local operator instance without account authentication. Its MCP uses your local operator access and does not need an API token.
settings.mcpLocalSteps: Run your MCP client on the same machine as Atoma and add the loopback address below using Streamable HTTP, without an Authorization header. A remote or cloud client cannot reach this loopback address.
settings.mcpApiMissing: The server did not find the token API (404). Reload Settings once. If it persists, ask the deployment administrator to update the API and web client together and check routing for /api/tokens and /mcp.
settings.mcpSignInAgain: Your Atoma session has expired. Sign in again, then reopen Settings.
settings.mcpForbidden: Your current account cannot perform this action. Check the selected organisation and ask its administrator to verify your access.
settings.mcpUnavailable: The request could not be completed. Check your connection and retry. If this continues, ask the deployment administrator to check the API service.
settings.mcpChangedRefreshFailed: The change was saved, but the token list could not be refreshed. Copy any new token now, then retry loading the list.
settings.mcpCheckSteps: In Claude Code or Codex, run /mcp and check that atoma is connected, then ask the agent to list your Atoma projects. In another client, refresh its MCP tools and try a read action. Creating a token alone does not establish a connection.
settings.mcpCheckUsage: The last-used date below updates after the client presents a valid token; reload Settings to refresh it. It does not prove a tool call succeeded. If atoma is already registered, edit or remove that existing client entry before adding it again.
settings.mcpTroubleshootAuth: 401: sign in again from your MCP client, or replace a lost or revoked manual token. 403: check organisation permissions and the MCP address. Revoking an access entry also blocks OAuth renewal.
settings.mcpTroubleshoot404: 404 on the first connection: check the complete /mcp address and server routing. 404 after a working session: reconnect the client to start a new MCP session. For OAuth discovery errors, check that /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server are reachable.
